claim: General fluid intelligence (gF) is a current problem-solving ability that shows high inter-individual differences in humans.
source: General fluid intelligence (gF) is a current problem-solving ability, which shows high inter-individual differences in humans (Cattell, 1963).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cattell, 1963

claim: Visuo-spatial intelligence is a key component of gF that shows high g-loading.
source: One key component of gF is visuo-spatial intelligence, usually tested by visual materials, shows high g-loading (Colom et al., 2006; Deary et al., 2010; Jung and Haier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colom et al., 2006; Deary et al., 2010; Jung and Haier, 2007

claim: The 'neuro-efficiency' hypothesis proposes that the human brain's ability to suppress irrelevant information leads to more efficient cognitive processing.
source: The 'neuro-efficiency' hypothesis is one explanation for individual differences in gF (Haier et al., 1988). This hypothesis puts forward that the human brain's ability to suppress irrelevant information leads to more efficient cognitive processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Haier et al., 1988

claim: There is a strong link between suppression index (SI) of motion perception and the scores of the block design test (BDT).
source: Correspondingly, using a well-known visual motion paradigm (center-surround antagonism; Liu et al., 2016; Tadin et al., 2003), Melnick et al. found a strong link between suppression index (SI) of motion perception and the scores of the block design test (BDT, a subtest of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale [WAIS]), which measures the visuo-spatial component (3D domain) of gF (Melnick et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016; Tadin et al., 2003; Melnick et al., 2013

claim: Motion surround suppression (SI) is a specific function of human extrastriate cortical region, middle temporal complex (hMT+).
source: Motion surround suppression (SI), a specific function of human extrastriate cortical region, middle temporal complex (hMT+), aligns closely with this region's activities (Gautama and Van Hulle, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gautama and Van Hulle, 2001

claim: hMT+ is a sensory cortex involved in visual perception processing (3D domain).
source: Furthermore, hMT+ is a sensory cortex involved in visual perception processing (3D domain; Cumming and DeAngelis, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cumming and DeAngelis, 2001

claim: Frontal cortex is usually recognized as the cognitive core region.
source: Frontal cortex is usually recognized as the cognitive core region (Duncan et al., 2000; Gray et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duncan et al., 2000; Gray et al., 2003

claim: Strong connectivity between cognitive regions suggests a mechanism for large-scale information exchange and integration in the brain.
source: Strong connectivity between the cognitive regions suggests a mechanism for large-scale information exchange and integration in the brain (Barbey, 2018; Cole et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barbey, 2018; Cole et al., 2012

claim: Ultra-high field (7T) magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) technology can reliably resolve GABA and Glu concentrations.
source: We employ ultra-high field (7T) magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) technology to reliably resolve GABA and Glu concentrations (Ende, 2015; Liu et al., 2022; Song et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ende, 2015; Liu et al., 2022; Song et al., 2021

claim: Early visual cortex (EVC, primarily in V1) mediates the 2D rather than 3D visual domain.
source: To verify the specificity of hMT+, we used early visual cortex (EVC, primarily in V1)-based GABA/Glu as control as it mediates the 2D rather than 3D visual domain (Cumming and DeAngelis, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cumming and DeAngelis, 2001

claim: GABAergic inhibition mechanisms (but not excitatory Glu) in hMT+ region relate to 3D visuo-spatial ability.
source: Our findings first demonstrate that GABAergic inhibition mechanisms (but not excitatory Glu) in hMT+ region relate to 3D visuo-spatial ability.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The network between MT+ and frontal cortex relating to MT+ GABA and perceptual suppression contributes to visuo-spatial intelligence.
source: Further, analysis of functional brain connectivity at rest reveals that the network (between MT+ and frontal cortex) relating to MT+ GABA and perceptual suppression contribute to the visuo-spatial intelligence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Thirty-six healthy subjects participated in this study.
source: Thirty-six healthy subjects (18 female, mean age: 23.6 years±2.1, range: 20–29 years) participated in this study, they were recruited from Zhejiang University.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: BDT significantly correlates with GABA concentrations in hMT+ voxels (r=0.39, p=0.03, n=31).
source: Quantitative analysis displayed that BDT significantly correlates with GABA concentrations in hMT+ voxels (r=0.39, p=0.03, n=31, Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3c

claim: After controlling for the effect of age, the relationship between BDT and GABA in hMT+ remains significant (rpartial = 0.426, p=0.02).
source: After using partial correlation to control for the effect of age, the relationship remains significant (rpartial = 0.426, p=0.02, one participant excluded due to the age greater than mean + 2.5 SD).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for age

claim: There was no obvious correlation between BDT and GABA levels in EVC (primarily in V1) voxels.
source: In contrast, there was no obvious correlation between BDT and GABA levels in EVC (primarily in V1) voxels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: SI significantly correlates with GABA levels in hMT+ voxels (r=0.44, p=0.01, n=31).
source: We show that SI significantly correlates with GABA levels in hMT+ voxels (r=0.44, p=0.01, n=31, Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3d

claim: No significant correlation between SI and GABA concentrations in EVC (primarily in V1) voxels was observed.
source: In contrast, no significant correlation between SI and GABA concentrations in EVC (primarily in V1) voxels was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b

claim: The relationship between motion suppression and GABA+ is specific to hMT+, but not in EVC (primarily in V1).
source: These findings suggest that the relationship between motion suppression and GABA+ is specific to hMT+, but not in EVC (primarily in V1), which is in line with prior results (Schallmo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Schallmo et al., 2018

claim: No significant correlations between BDT and Glu levels were found in both hMT+ and EVC (primarily in V1) voxels.
source: Unlike in the case of GABA, no significant correlations between BDT and Glu levels were found in both hMT+ and EVC (primarily in V1) voxels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b and c

claim: Significant positive correlations between GABA and Glu concentrations were observed in both hMT+ (r=0.62, p=0.0002, n=31) and EVC (primarily in V1) voxels (r=0.56, p=0.002, n=28).
source: While, as expected (Song et al., 2021), we observed significant positive correlations between GABA and Glu concentrations in both hMT+ (r=0.62, p=0.0002, n=31) and EVC (primarily in V1) voxels (r=0.56, p=0.002, n=28; Figure 3—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a and b, and citation to Song et al., 2021

claim: Significant correlations between SI and BDT were discerned (r=0.59, p=0.0002, n=34).
source: Additionally, significant correlations between SI and BDT, duration threshold of small grating and BDT was discerned (r=0.59, p=0.0002, n=34, Figure 3e, rpartial = 0.67, p<0.001, one participant excluded due to the age greater than mean + 2.5 SD; r=–0.43, p=0.016, rpartial = 0.44, p=0.014, Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3e

claim: Significant correlation between duration threshold of small grating and BDT was found (r=–0.43, p=0.016).
source: Additionally, significant correlations between SI and BDT, duration threshold of small grating and BDT was discerned (r=0.59, p=0.0002, n=34, Figure 3e, rpartial = 0.67, p<0.001, one participant excluded due to the age greater than mean + 2.5 SD; r=–0.43, p=0.016, rpartial = 0.44, p=0.014, Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3f

claim: There was no significant correlation between duration threshold of large grating and BDT.
source: While there was no significant correlation between duration threshold of large grating and BDT (Figure 3g), corroborating previous conclusions (Melnick et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis, Figure 3g, and citation to Melnick et al., 2013

claim: Brain regions with FC strength to the seed region (left hMT+) significantly correlated with BDT scores were situated within the canonical cognitive cores of fronto-parietal network (FPN) (Brodmann areas [BAs] 6, 9, 10, 46, 47).
source: We found that brain regions with FC strength to the seed region (left hMT+) significantly correlated with BDT scores were situated within the canonical cognitive cores of fronto-parietal network (FPN) (Brodmann areas [BAs] 6, 9, 10, 46, 47; Assem et al., 2020; Deary et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2020; Duncan et al., 2000; Gray et al., 2003; Jung and Haier, 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Assem et al., 2020; Deary et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2020; Duncan et al., 2000; Gray et al., 2003; Jung and Haier, 2007

claim: Certain parietal regions (BAs 7, 39, 40) showed significant correlations between their connectivity to the left hMT+ and the BDT scores.
source: Additionally, we identified certain parietal regions (BAs 7, 39, 40) with significant correlations between their connectivity to the left hMT+ and the BDT scores (Supplementary file 1; also shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: FC-SI analysis in the frontal regions displayed three brain regions in which FCs strength significantly correlated with SI: right BA4/6, left BA6, and right BA46.
source: Our FC-SI analysis in the frontal regions (a priori search space) displayed three brain regions in which FCs strength significantly correlated with SI: right BA4/6, left BA6, and right BA46 (summarized in Supplementary file 2, and shown in Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 4b

claim: Only two FCs significantly correlated with inhibitory GABA levels in hMT+: (1) the FC of left hMT+-right BA46 (significantly negative correlation, r = –0.56, p=0.02, n=29, FDR correction); (2) the FC of left hMT+-right BA6 (significantly positive correlation, r=0.69, p=0.002, n=29, FDR correction).
source: The results revealed that only two FCs significantly correlated with inhibitory GABA levels in hMT+: (1) the FC of left hMT+-right BA46 (significantly negative correlation, r = –0.56, p=0.02, n=29, false discovery rate [FDR] correction, Figure 5a left); (2) the FC of left hMT+-right BA6 (significantly positive correlation, r=0.69, p=0.002, n=29, FDR correction, Figure 5b left; also shown in Table 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis, Figure 5a and 5b, and Table 2

claim: There were no significant correlations between these FCs and the excitatory Glu levels in hMT+.
source: There were no significant correlations between these FCs and the excitatory Glu levels in hMT+ (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Table 2

claim: The hypothesized indirect effect (i.e. hMT+ GABA → FC of hMT+-BA46 → SI → BDT) was significant (β=2.28, SE = 1.54, 95% CI = [0.03, 5.94]).
source: Critically, bootstrapped analyses revealed that our hypothesized indirect effect (i.e. hMT+ GABA → FC of hMT+-BA46 → SI → BDT) was significant (β=2.28, SE = 1.54, 95% CI = [0.03, 5.94]).
evidence: Supported by statistical mediation analysis

claim: The serial mediation model accounted for 34% of the variance in BDT.
source: The model accounted for 34% of the variance in BDT.
evidence: Supported by statistical mediation analysis

claim: The hMT-BA6 FC totally mediates the relationship between GABA and BDS.
source: Consequently, we explored a mediation model, which revealed that the hMT-BA6 FC totally mediates the relationship between GABA and BDS (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by statistical mediation analysis and Figure 5d

claim: Higher GABAergic inhibition in hMT+ relates to stronger negative FC between hMT+ and BA46, leading to enhanced ability for surround suppression, which ultimately results in more efficient visual 3D processing as key component of gF.
source: That is, higher GABAergic inhibition in hMT+ relates to stronger negative FC between hMT+ and BA46, leading to enhanced ability for surround suppression (filtering out irrelevant information; Tadin, 2015), which ultimately resulting in more efficient visual 3D processing as key component of gF (the higher BDT scores).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Tadin, 2015

claim: Inhibitory mechanisms in hMT+, from the biochemical level of GABA over FC to the behavioral level, can predict the inter-subject variance in the 3D gF task (BDT).
source: Thereby, our data indicate that inhibitory mechanisms in hMT+, from the biochemical level of GABA over FC to the behavioral level, can predict the inter-subject variance in the 3D gF task (BDT; Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 5c

claim: GABAergic inhibition in hMT+ couples with distinct FC patterns between BA46-hMT+ and BA6-hMT+.
source: Another interesting finding reveals that GABAergic inhibition in hMT+ coupling with distinct FC patterns between BA46-hMT+ and BA6-hMT+.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Selective attention gates the visual cortex, including area MT, effectively suppressing the irrelevant information.
source: Monkey electrophysiological experiments revealed that selective attention gates the visual cortex, including area MT, effectively suppressing the irrelevant information (Everling et al., 2002; Treue and Maunsell, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Everling et al., 2002; Treue and Maunsell, 1996

claim: Neural suppression is associated with the balance between excitation and inhibition (EIB), usually represented by covariation between Glu and GABA.
source: Neural suppression is associated with the balance between excitation and inhibition (EIB), usually represented by covariation between Glu and GABA (Ozeki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozeki et al., 2009

claim: The conjoint action of inhibition (GABA) and excitation (Glu) underlies visual spatial suppression.
source: Our recent human study (Song et al., 2021) and other study's animal experiments Ozeki et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2016 demonstrated that the conjoint action of inhibition (GABA) and excitation (Glu) underlies visual spatial suppression.
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2021; Ozeki et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2016

claim: Positive and negative correlations between BDT and the activation of frontal regions appeared at different reasoning phases (validation or integration phases during reasoning).
source: A previous human fMRI experiment found that the positive and negative correlations between BDT and the activation of frontal regions appeared at different reasoning phases (validation or integration phases during reasoning; Fangmeier et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fangmeier et al., 2006

claim: Delayed modulation from PFC (especially in DLPFC; BA46) to area MT occurs during a visual motion task.
source: On the one hand, a monkey electrophysiological experiment reported the delayed modulation from PFC (especially in DLPFC; BA46) to area MT during a visual motion task (Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006

claim: Computational models converged with empirical data of awake monkey experiments showing temporal modulation from PFC to MT/medial superior temporal (MST).
source: Computational models converged with empirical data of awake monkey experiments slowing temporal modulation from PFC to MT/medial superior temporal (MST; Donner et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2015; Wang, 2002; Wimmer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donner et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2015; Wang, 2002; Wimmer et al., 2015

claim: Gamma-band activity in the visual cortex (including area MT) exhibited high coherence with the activity in (pre-) motor regions (BA4/6).
source: On the other hand, human MEG studies (Donner et al., 2009; Wilming et al., 2020) reported that the gamma-band activity in the visual cortex (including area MT) exhibited high coherence with the activity in (pre-) motor regions (BA4/6).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donner et al., 2009; Wilming et al., 2020

claim: The overlap brain regions from the analyses of connectivity-BDT-GABA/connectivity-SI-GABA are the hMT+-BA46.
source: The results in Figure 5a and b showed that the overlap brain regions from the analyses of connectivity-BDT-GABA/connectivity-SI-GABA are the hMT+-BA46.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 5a and b

claim: Both local (FC within BA18) and global brain connectivity (FC between hMT+ and frontal regions) contribute to SI.
source: However, our results with connectivity-SI analyses revealed that both local (FC within BA18) and global brain connectivity (FC between hMT+ and frontal regions) contribute to SI (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 3

claim: Brief stimulus duration (~100 ms) in motion discrimination precludes most top-down attentional effects.
source: In human psychophysical experiments (Melnick et al., 2013; Tadin et al., 2003) the brief stimulus duration (~100 ms) in motion discrimination precludes most top-down attentional effects (Wang, 2002; Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006), while attention, which predicted the performance of the motion discrimination task, was sustained throughout the stimulus intervals (Siegel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melnick et al., 2013; Tadin et al., 2003; Wang, 2002; Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006; Siegel et al., 2015

claim: Local circuits in the visual cortex combining with top-down modulation and intracortical horizontal connection mediate the visual-spatial suppression.
source: Furthermore, animal experiments have revealed that the local circuits in the visual cortex combining with top-down modulation and intracortical horizontal connection mediate the visual-spatial suppression (Angelucci et al., 2002; Keller et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Angelucci et al., 2002; Keller et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014

claim: A candidate divisive normalization model can explain how reverberation affects the process of suppressing the irrelevant information, from perception to intelligence.
source: A candidate divisive normalization model (Carandini and Heeger, 2011; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009) can explain how such reverberation affects the process of suppressing the irrelevant information, from perception to intelligence (Melnick et al., 2013; Tadin, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carandini and Heeger, 2011; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Melnick et al., 2013; Tadin, 2015

claim: The MD system encompasses a range of cognitive domains, including working memory, mathematics, language, and relational reasoning.
source: The MD system encompasses a range of cognitive domains, including working memory, mathematics, language, and relational reasoning.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section

claim: Motion surround suppression (SI) and time thresholds for small and large gratings, which reflect hMT+ functionality, are correlated with Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed indicators.
source: According to Melnick et al., 2013, motion surround suppression (SI) and time thresholds for small and large gratings, which reflect hMT+ functionality, are correlated with Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed indicators.
evidence: Supported by citation to Melnick et al., 2013

claim: Fedorenko et al. identified MD activation regions around the occipito-temporal areas, potentially overlapping with hMT+.
source: Additionally, Fedorenko et al. identified MD activation regions around the occipito-temporal areas, potentially overlapping with hMT+ (Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fedorenko et al., 2013

claim: hMT+ is a key region in the representation of sensory flows (including optic and auditory flows).
source: As a key region in the representation of sensory flows (including optic and auditory flows; Fetsch et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2006), hMT+ shows potential to be central to the MD system.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fetsch et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2006

claim: The information exchange and integration between the sensory cortex (hMT+) and cognition core of BA46, coupling with the hMT+ GABA, can predict the performance of 3D visuo-spatial ability (BDT).
source: Together, this study offers a comprehensive insight into how the information exchange and integration between the sensory cortex (hMT+) and cognition core of BA46, coupling with the hMT+ GABA, can predict the performance of 3D visuo-spatial ability (BDT).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A sensory cortex area (hMT+), its GABA biochemistry, FC, and cognition behavior levels can assemble into complex cognition as an intellectual hub.
source: Our results provide direct evidence that a sensory cortex area (hMT+), its GABA biochemistry, FC, and cognition behavior levels can assemble into complex cognition as an intellectual hub.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript
